extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges dealing with assignments, grants, and joint-ownership of patents
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrines governing assignments, conditional assignments, grants vs licenses, rights to sue for past infringements, estoppel, and the rights/duties of joint-owners of patents. Focused on transfer and ownership consequences rather than prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel of patentee in suit by assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is estopped from denying the validity of the patent or its re-issues in a suit brought against him by his assignee, even though the re-issues were granted after the assignment, if the assignee ought to have known they were void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Burdsall v. Curran (1887), Joliet Wire Check Power Co. (1886). Explanatory note: an assignee who brings suit is protected from the assignor's later attacks on validity when the assignee has continued to treat the patent as valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant estopped to deny deed of assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is estopped from denying his deed of assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Edison (1875). Applied where applicant has executed an assignment and later attempts to repudiate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller cannot defeat assignee by buying older patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee having sold his patent cannot defeat his assignee's rights by subsequently buying an older patent and claiming that it renders the assignee's patent invalid or inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Rumsey v. Buck (1884), Curran v. Burdsall (1883). The asignor's later acquisition of prior art patents does not defeat earlier conveyances to assignees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of junior patent becomes licensee of co-owners of older patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an assignor is co-owner of an older and superior patent, the assignee of the junior patent becomes the licensee of the other co-owners and must look to the assignor for compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Curran v. Burdsall (1883). Practical effect: assignee cannot claim full freedom if assignor lacks exclusive title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor who agreed to stop making cannot deny validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an assignor agreed to stop making the invention and paid a license fee to the assignee for the privilege of selling what he had on hand, he cannot later deny the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates estoppel where assignor accepted consideration and agreed to refrain from use/sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee taking and enjoying benefits is estopped from denying patent or assignor's title
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, by the terms of assignment, the assignee becomes liable for royalties or a share of profits and has taken and still enjoys the benefits of the assignment, he is estopped from denying the patent's validity or the title conferred by the assignor in an action for an account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignee repudiates and relinquishes benefits upon discovering defects, the estoppel ceases to operate. Cases and notes cited in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee cannot offset royalties by alleging fraud in assignor after receiving benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee cannot defend against a claim for royalties on the ground of fraud on the assignor if he has received all benefits of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Shaw v. Soule (1884). Emphasizes that receipt of assignment benefits triggers estoppel against certain defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee manufacturing under terms cannot deny validity when called to account
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee who manufactures on terms (i.e., pursuant to agreement) cannot deny the validity of the patent when called to an account for royalties or profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Kinsman v. Parkhurst (1855). Practical effect for accounting actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee cannot buy a claim against patentee and set it off
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee cannot purchase from a third person a claim against the patentee and set it up as a set-off against amounts due under the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Kinsman v. Parkhurst (1855). Prevents assignees from undermining assignor's recovery by buying stale claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recital of vendor's ownership in conditional contract not estoppel if rescinded
rubrics_metrics.description: A recital in a conditional contract of assignment that 'the vendor is the owner of the patent' is not an estoppel on the purchaser if the contract is rescinded before it takes effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Swift v. Bochow (1880). Caveat: estoppel depends on whether the contract has become effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional assignments create reversionary interests
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment may be made upon condition or for a term less than the patent's full duration, creating reversionary interests in the assignor which he can protect and enforce by legal or equitable actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Otis Bros. Mfg. Co. v. Crane Bros. (1886), Still v. Reading (1881). If conditions are unfulfilled, assignor retains remedy and title may revert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term assignments leave reversionary interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment for a term of years leaves a reversionary interest in the assignor which he can protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Still v. Reading (1881). Common law protection of reserved reversionary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether condition subsequent defeated is a court question
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether a conditional assignment or a condition subsequent has been defeated is one for the courts to decide, not the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Hammond v. Pratt (1880). Patent Office does not adjudicate contractual condition fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale with reconveyance condition is enforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is sold with a condition of reconveyance, the condition may be enforced by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Andrews v. Fielding (1884). Typical equitable remedy enforcing reconveyance clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to carry out contractual purpose may cause reversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the assignee fails to carry out the purpose for which the patent was assigned and the contract provides for reversion in such a case, the patent will revert to the assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Buckley v. Sawyer Mfg. Co. (1881). Enforced when express contractual reversion terms exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: After forfeiture by breach of condition assignee can grant nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: After an assignment has been forfeited by breach of condition, the assignee can grant nothing either by way of license or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Abbett v. Zusi (1879). Forfeiture terminates assignee's power to convey rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignees subject to assignor's prior acts known to them
rubrics_metrics.description: Privity between assignor and assignees makes assignees subject to legal consequences of the assignor's prior acts of which they had actual or constructive notice; judgments rendered against assignor before assignment conclude assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Worley v. Tobacco Co. (1881), McClurg v. Kingsland (1843). Key: notice (actual or constructive) is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private conduct of assignor unknown to assignee does not bind assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: Private conduct or admissions of the assignor, of which assignees could not have obtained information or were not bound to inquire, do not affect the assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts subsequent to assignment cannot prejudice assignee's rights; protects bona fide purchasers without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser during interference bound by caveat emptor
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser who buys an interest in an invention during an interference is bound by the rule of caveat emptor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Mason (1872). Purchaser must beware of pending disputes over priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of an assignee takes no greater rights than grantor had
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee of the interest of another assignee takes no more than his grantor had and is charged with whatever notice he might have learned from the original grantor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Hamilton v. Kingsbury (1880). Chain-of-title principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee concluded by decree against assignor
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignee of a patent is concluded by a decree entered against his assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Pennington v. Hunt (1884). Decrees in suits binding on successors who had notice or privity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee takes subject to assignor's disclaimers and estoppels
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee takes subject to the assignor's disclaimers and other acts working an estoppel of which the assignee had knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Blades v. Rand, McNally & Co. (1886). Knowledge/constructive notice determine burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee who assigns his rights binds his assignee by known equities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an assignee assigns his rights, his assignee is bound by all the equities of which the first assignee had knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain-of-equities: purchasers must inquire into existing equities in the chain of title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to sue for past infringements is assignable
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to sue for past infringements may be assigned in connection with an assignment of the patent, and the assignee can enforce the remedy at law or equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No especial form required; assignment after suit commenced requires notifying defendant before further proceedings. Instruments (e.g., irrevocable POA) executed after patent expiry can be sufficient for collecting past claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of share of suit proceeds creates no interest in patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a share in the proceeds of suits for infringements creates no interest in the invention or the monopoly itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Tilghman v. Proctor (1888). Distinguishes financial assignments from transfers of substantive patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of action survives to personal representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A right of action for infringement survives to personal representatives and may be sued on or assigned by them (if local law permits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: May v. County of Logan (1887). Administrators may sue/assign under applicable local rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of expired patent affects only past-claim rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of an expired patent can take effect only as an assignment of claims for past infringements; it does not create ongoing patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: May v. Saginaw Co. (1887). Practical limit on what can be conveyed after expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment by administrator may carry past-infringement claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment by an administrator of all rights under or through an expired patent carries claims for past infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: May v. Saginaw Co. (1887). Executors/administrators can transfer claim rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant distinguished from assignment by territorial scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant differs from an assignment only as to the territorial limits within which it operates: a conveyance operative throughout the entire United States is an assignment; a conveyance confined to a particular locality is a grant (state/right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination turns on whether the conveyance is of force throughout the entire United States or confined to a locality; positive or negative phrasing of restrictions is immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant distinguished from license by nature of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: To distinguish a grant from a license, regard the nature of the interest conveyed: a grant conveys the exclusive interest in the invention and the monopoly within prescribed limits and permits suit in the grantee's own name; a license conveys a non-exclusive or partial interest and normally does not permit suit in licensee's own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory basis: Rev. Stat. sec. 4898 allowing grant of exclusive rights as to specified parts of the U.S. Practical test: exclusivity of the interest and ability to sue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of all patentee's interest in a territory is a grant
rubrics_metrics.description: A transfer of all the patentee's interest in a given territory is a grant (exclusive territorial right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Perry v. Corning (1870). If rights to make/use/sell in the territory are exclusive and cover the rights mentioned in the patent, it's a grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑exclusive right is an interest in the invention, not the monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exclusive right is an interest in the invention (a license), distinguished from the monopoly which must be exclusive to constitute a grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant must operate on rights to make, use, and sell and be exclusive as to all three; absence of exclusivity indicates license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants can be conditional or limited in enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant, like an assignment, may be conditional or temporary and may be limited as to the extent of its enjoyment (for example, exclusive right to make a certain number of devices within territory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such limited grants still confer exclusive territorial interest despite short-term or quantitative restrictions (cases: Bitter v. Serrell (1852)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on mode of use/sale do not necessarily make conveyance a license
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant may be limited as to the mode of using the invention or the sale of its products outside the territory and still be a grant, unless the enjoyment is denied to the grantee and reserved to the grantor or another alienee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If restrictions are merely limits on exercise but the grantee alone holds exclusive rights in the area, it's still a grant; absent reservation, grantee's exclusive right remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial grantee's vendee may use devices anywhere where conveyance so allows
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patentee grants a territorial right to make/use/sell without limiting the use by vendees, the vendees of the grantee may use the invention anywhere in the U.S. without reference to other grants of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Adams v. Burke (1873). Practical consequence for downstream purchasers' freedom of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of territorial right cannot make for use outside his territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A grantee cannot make the device outside his own territory for use outside it; territorial assignments constrain where manufacture and intended use may occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: American Paper Barrel Co. v. Lanway (1886); Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Nixon (1876). But unrestricted territorial assignees may sell devices for use anywhere in some cases (Hatch v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation of use in one assigned State does not affect assignee's rights in others
rubrics_metrics.description: The reservation by an assignor of the right to use the invention in one of several assigned States does not affect the assignee's rights in the other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Hobbie v. Smith (1886). Territorial reservations are narrowly applied to the specified area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant must be written, signed, and recorded to affect subsequent bona fide grantees
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant must be in writing and duly signed by the grantor and must be recorded within the statutory period to avail against subsequent bona fide assignees and grantees for value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute cited: Rev. Stat. sec. 4898. Recording is necessary to give constructive notice to subsequent purchasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant imports warranty of title and gives rise to estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant imports a warranty of title and gives rise to the same estoppel and privities of interest and obligation as an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal consequence: grantee may rely on warranty; estoppel prevents grantor/grantee from certain later contradictory assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveyance of 'all right title and interest' does not cut off prior recorded territorial rights of grantor
rubrics_metrics.description: A conveyance of 'all my right, title, and interest' in and to a patent, though recorded, does not affect territorial or temporal rights previously conveyed by the grantor and not recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Turnbull v. Weir Plow Co. (1880). Recording timing and existing unrecorded grants affect priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: If grantee avails himself of grant cannot deny true inventor unless evicted
rubrics_metrics.description: If a grantee avails himself of the grant, he cannot, in a suit for royalties on goods sold, deny that the patentee is the true inventor unless he has been evicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Birdsall v. Perrigo (1865). Using the grant typically precludes later attack on title absent eviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of undivided interest creates joint-ownership in invention and monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: By assignment of an undivided interest in a patented invention, the assignor and assignee become joint-owners both of the invention and of the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint-ownership raises unique problems because the monopoly is incorporeal and indivisible in practical effect; courts have struggled with rules governing co-owners' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three conceptual rules for joint-owners' relation to monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Three possible rules describe joint-owners' relation: (1) each owner individually possesses the monopoly; (2) each individually possesses invention rights while monopoly resides entire in owners collectively (favored); (3) rights and monopoly vest indivisibly in all as a single person (rejected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise favors second rule as preserving monopoly character while allowing individual practice; courts have sometimes applied aspects of the first rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-owners are not co-partners; interests are distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-owners of a patent are not co-partners or collective owners in the partnership sense; their interests are distinct and independent though subject to monopoly limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to tenants in common and chattel law is limited; many partnership doctrines do not apply to patent joint-ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under favored rule co-owners may individually practise and convey own share but cannot multiply transferees/licences to the prejudice of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the second (preferred) rule, each co-owner may practise the invention and convey his interest to another without accounting to co-owners, but assignment of one owner's interest to many transferees or granting multiple licenses that multiply practicing persons may sensibly diminish the patent's value to co-owners and is restricted in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions vary: some adopt first-rule consequences (allowing abrogation of monopoly by transfer) but typically limit harm by requiring accounting for proceeds to co-owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-owners' remedies when one converts or destroys joint property
rubrics_metrics.description: If one joint-owner destroys or sells the joint property (e.g., appropriates exclusive right), co-owners may have remedies such as actions for conversion or account; purchasers from a co-owner become tenants in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to common law trover and tenants in common; cases: Dunham v. Indianapolis & St. Louis R. Co. (1876). Practical rights include seeking share of proceeds or damages.
